courses.title: 1. Load balancing fundamentals: L4 vs L7
courses.summary: What a load balancer does, the difference between layer-4 and layer-7 balancing, and the reverse-proxy model behind every modern web stack.
courses.expected: Run behind two backends on a Docker network: repeated `curl localhost:8080` responses alternate between web1 and web2, proving traffic is spread across both.

lessons.title: What a load balancer does
paragraphs: A load balancer is the single entry point that spreads incoming requests across a pool of backend servers. It lets you scale horizontally (add servers instead of a bigger one), survive a server failing, and deploy without downtime.
Clients only ever see the load balancer's address; the pool behind it can grow, shrink or be replaced without the client knowing. This indirection is the foundation of every scalable web service.
lessons.example: Clients -> one LB address -> many interchangeable backends behind it.
lessons.pitfall: Pointing clients directly at individual backends defeats the purpose: you lose failover and can't scale or redeploy transparently.

question.prompt: A load balancer lets you scale by:

options.text: adding interchangeable backends behind one address

question.explanation: Horizontal scale behind one entry point.

lessons.title: Layer 4 vs layer 7
paragraphs: A layer-4 (transport) load balancer routes by IP address and TCP/UDP port without looking inside the connection. It is fast and protocol-agnostic but cannot make decisions based on the request's content.

A layer-7 (application) load balancer terminates the connection and understands HTTP, so it can route by hostname, path, header or cookie, do TLS termination, and rewrite requests. It is more capable but does more work per request.
lessons.example: L4: route by IP:port (fast). L7: route by Host/path/header (smart).
lessons.pitfall: Expecting a pure L4 balancer to route by URL path is impossible — it never parses HTTP; you need L7 for that.

question.prompt: Routing by URL path or hostname requires:

lessons.title: The reverse-proxy model
paragraphs: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and forwards client requests to them, the opposite of a forward proxy that sits in front of clients. An L7 load balancer is a reverse proxy that also chooses among several backends.
Because it terminates the client connection, a reverse proxy can add TLS, compression, caching, request buffering and header rewriting in one place, centralising cross-cutting concerns.
lessons.example: A reverse proxy terminates the client connection and forwards to a chosen backend.
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting to forward the real client address (X-Forwarded-For) makes every backend log see the proxy's IP instead of the user's.

question.prompt: A reverse proxy sits in front of:

lessons.title: Availability and scaling
paragraphs: With a pool behind the balancer, one backend failing just means its share of traffic shifts to the others — if the balancer detects the failure. Rolling deployments drain one backend at a time so users never hit a server mid-restart.
The load balancer itself must not become a single point of failure: production setups run it redundantly (active-passive or active-active) with a floating/virtual IP or a cloud-managed LB.
lessons.example: The LB removes single points of failure among backends, but must itself be redundant.
lessons.pitfall: Running a single load-balancer instance recreates the single point of failure you were trying to remove.

courses.title: 2. Balancing algorithms and session affinity
courses.summary: Round-robin, weighted, least-connections and hashing, plus consistent hashing and sticky sessions for stateful backends.
courses.expected: With the weights above and round-robin, roughly three of every four requests hit web1 and one hits web2 (a 3:1 split).

lessons.title: Round-robin and weighted
paragraphs: Round-robin sends each new request to the next backend in turn — simple, even, and the default in most balancers. Weighted round-robin biases the rotation so more powerful backends receive proportionally more traffic.
Round-robin assumes requests cost about the same. When some requests are far heavier than others, an even rotation can still overload one backend.
lessons.example: weight=3 on a server gives it roughly three times the share of a weight=1 peer.
lessons.pitfall: Using plain round-robin when request costs vary wildly can pile expensive requests onto one node despite the even count.

question.prompt: Weighted round-robin is used when backends:

lessons.title: Least-connections and least-time
paragraphs: Least-connections sends each request to the backend currently handling the fewest active connections, adapting to real load rather than assuming requests are equal. It suits workloads with varying request durations.
Variants like least-time (NGINX Plus/other proxies) also factor in response latency. These adaptive policies beat round-robin when request cost is uneven.
lessons.example: least_conn routes to whichever backend has the fewest in-flight requests right now.
lessons.pitfall: Least-connections across backends with very different capacities still needs weights, or the small node gets overwhelmed at equal connection counts.

question.prompt: Least-connections adapts to:

lessons.title: Hashing and consistent hashing
paragraphs: Hash-based policies route by hashing a key (client IP, URL, header) so the same key always lands on the same backend — useful for cache locality. Plain hash%N, though, reshuffles almost every key when the backend count changes.
Consistent hashing fixes this: adding or removing a backend remaps only a small fraction of keys, so a cache tier stays mostly warm during scaling. NGINX exposes it with `hash <key> consistent`.
lessons.example: hash $request_uri consistent;  # same URL -> same backend, minimal remap on change
lessons.pitfall: Using plain (non-consistent) hashing for a cache tier causes a near-total cache miss storm whenever you add or remove a node.

question.prompt: Consistent hashing is preferred for caches because on scaling it:
question.explanation: It keeps most keys (and caches) in place.

lessons.title: Session affinity (sticky sessions)
paragraphs: A stateful backend that keeps a user's session in local memory needs that user's requests to keep returning to it — session affinity. It is done by hashing the client IP (ip_hash) or by a cookie the balancer sets and reads.

Stickiness undermines even balancing and complicates failover (a dead backend loses its sessions). The better long-term fix is to make backends stateless by storing session state in a shared store (Redis, a database).
lessons.example: ip_hash or a sticky cookie pins a user to one backend; stateless backends avoid the need.
lessons.pitfall: Relying on sticky sessions as your scaling strategy means a backend failure logs out everyone pinned to it.

question.prompt: The cleanest alternative to sticky sessions is:

options.text: stateless backends with shared session storage

steps: Save the downloaded lb-algorithms.conf and run nginx with it mounted at /etc/nginx/nginx.conf (`-v $PWD/lb-algorithms.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro`), behind two whoami backends (web1, web2) on a Docker network.
With the default (weighted round-robin), curl repeatedly and confirm web1 answers about 3x as often as web2.
Uncomment `ip_hash` and confirm one client keeps hitting the same backend.
Uncomment `hash $request_uri consistent` and confirm the same URL always goes to the same backend.

courses.title: 3. Health checks, timeouts and resilience
courses.summary: Active vs passive health checks, timeouts and retries, connection draining, and circuit breaking so one sick backend doesn't sink the service.
courses.expected: A backend that errors or times out is retried on another backend and, after 3 failures, ejected for 30s; healthy traffic keeps flowing without the client seeing the failure.

lessons.title: Active vs passive health checks
paragraphs: Passive health checks observe real traffic: if a backend returns errors or times out enough times, the balancer stops sending it requests for a while. NGINX open-source uses this model (max_fails / fail_timeout).

Active health checks probe each backend on a schedule (e.g. GET /healthz) regardless of traffic, so a dead backend is detected before a user hits it. HAProxy does this in open source; in NGINX it requires Plus or a module.
lessons.example: Passive: learn from failed real requests. Active: probe /healthz on a timer.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming open-source NGINX does active health checks is wrong — it only has passive; HAProxy OSS has active checks.

question.prompt: Open-source NGINX health checking is:

lessons.title: Readiness vs liveness
paragraphs: A readiness check answers 'can this instance take traffic right now?' — fail it and the balancer stops routing, without killing the instance. A liveness check answers 'is this instance wedged and need restarting?'.
Separating them matters: a backend warming a cache should be not-ready (kept out of rotation) but still alive (not restarted). Conflating them causes needless restart loops.
lessons.example: Readiness -> remove from rotation; liveness -> restart the instance.
lessons.pitfall: Using a liveness check for a slow-starting app restarts it mid-warmup forever; it should fail readiness instead.

question.prompt: A backend warming up should fail:

lessons.title: Timeouts and retries
paragraphs: Every hop needs bounded timeouts: connect, send and read. Without them a single stuck backend ties up balancer resources until exhaustion. On a failed or timed-out request, the balancer can retry the next backend.
Retries must be bounded and, ideally, only for idempotent requests — blindly retrying a non-idempotent POST can double-submit. A retry budget prevents a retry storm from amplifying an outage.
lessons.example: proxy_connect_timeout / proxy_read_timeout + a bounded proxy_next_upstream_tries.
lessons.pitfall: Retrying non-idempotent requests (like a payment POST) on timeout can charge the customer twice.

question.prompt: Automatic retries are safe mainly for:

lessons.title: Draining and circuit breaking
paragraphs: Connection draining removes a backend from rotation for new requests while letting in-flight requests finish, so a deploy or scale-down doesn't drop live connections. It is the graceful counterpart to adding a backend.

A circuit breaker trips when a backend's error rate is high, failing fast instead of hammering it, then probes for recovery. Together, draining and circuit breaking keep one sick backend from degrading the whole service.
lessons.example: Drain = finish in-flight, accept no new; circuit breaker = fail fast on a sick backend.
lessons.pitfall: Scaling down a backend without draining it kills every in-flight request on that instance.

question.prompt: Connection draining lets a backend being removed:

options.text: finish in-flight requests while taking no new ones

courses.title: 4. Hands-on: NGINX reverse proxy and upstreams
courses.summary: Build a complete NGINX load balancer in Docker: an upstream group, proxy headers, timeouts and fail-over, tested against real backends.
courses.expected: `docker exec lb nginx -t` reports the config is valid; `curl localhost:8080` alternates between web1 and web2 by least-connections, and `curl localhost:8080/healthz` returns ok.

lessons.title: The nginx.conf structure
paragraphs: An NGINX config is a tree of directives and blocks. The top level needs an `events {}` block (connection processing) and an `http {}` block for web traffic. Inside http you define `upstream` groups and `server` blocks (virtual servers).
A `server` block listens on a port and contains `location` blocks that match request paths. Omitting the mandatory `events {}` block makes `nginx -t` reject the file.
lessons.example: Top level: events { } and http { }; inside http: upstream { } and server { }.
lessons.pitfall: A full nginx.conf without a top-level `events {}` block fails `nginx -t` with an 'events directive is not allowed / missing' style error.

question.prompt: A complete nginx.conf must contain a top-level:

lessons.title: Upstream groups
paragraphs: An `upstream` block names a pool of backends and sets the policy; `proxy_pass http://<name>` in a location forwards to that pool. Each `server` line can carry a weight, a backup flag and passive health parameters.
NGINX resolves upstream server hostnames when it loads the config, so on a Docker network the backend names must be resolvable (the containers must exist on the same network).
lessons.example: upstream backend { least_conn; server web1:80; server web2:80; }  proxy_pass http://backend;
lessons.pitfall: Referencing a backend hostname that NGINX can't resolve at load time makes the whole config fail to start.

question.prompt: proxy_pass http://backend forwards to:

lessons.title: Proxy headers
paragraphs: When NGINX proxies a request it should pass through the information the backend needs: `Host` (the original hostname), `X-Forwarded-For` (the client's real IP, appended) and `X-Forwarded-Proto` (http/https). Without them, backends see the proxy, not the user.
These headers are how backends do correct logging, generate correct absolute URLs, and know whether the original request was HTTPS even after TLS was terminated at the proxy.
lessons.example: proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting X-Forwarded-Proto makes an app behind a TLS-terminating proxy build http:// redirect URLs and create redirect loops.

question.prompt: X-Forwarded-For carries the:

lessons.title: Running and testing it
paragraphs: You run NGINX in Docker by mounting your nginx.conf into the official image on the same network as the backends: `-v $PWD/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro`. Always validate first with `nginx -t` before reloading.
`nginx -s reload` applies a new config without dropping connections. In production you change the config, test it, then reload — never restart under live traffic if a reload will do.
lessons.example: docker run -v $PWD/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro nginx:1.27-alpine; nginx -t; nginx -s reload
lessons.pitfall: Reloading a config you didn't `nginx -t` first can take the proxy down if the new file has a syntax error.

question.prompt: Before reloading NGINX you should run:

steps: Create the network and backends: `docker network create lb`; run `web1` and `web2` from `traefik/whoami` on it.
Save the downloaded lb-nginx.conf and start NGINX: `docker run -d --name lb --network lb -p 8080:80 -v $PWD/lb-nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro nginx:1.27-alpine`.
Validate and test: `docker exec lb nginx -t`, then `curl -s localhost:8080` repeatedly and `curl localhost:8080/healthz`.
Stop web1 and confirm fail-over to web2 with no client-visible errors.

courses.title: 5. Hands-on: HAProxy with active health checks
courses.summary: Build an HAProxy load balancer with a frontend/backend split, active health checks, balancing policy and a live stats page.
courses.code:
# haproxy.cfg -- frontend/backend load balancer with ACTIVE health checks (a
# first-class open-source HAProxy feature). Mount at /usr/local/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg.
global
    log stdout format raw local0
    maxconn 4096

defaults
    mode http
    log global
    option httplog
    timeout connect 5s
    timeout client  30s
    timeout server  30s
    retries 2

frontend web
    bind *:80
    default_backend servers

backend servers
    balance roundrobin
    option httpchk GET /health            # the active health-check request
    http-check expect status 200
    server web1 web1:80 check inter 2s fall 3 rise 2   # check every 2s
    server web2 web2:80 check inter 2s fall 3 rise 2

listen stats
    bind *:8404
    stats enable
    stats uri /stats                      # live dashboard at :8404/stats
courses.expected: `haproxy -c -f haproxy.cfg` reports the config is valid; traffic round-robins across healthy backends, a failed backend is removed within a few check intervals, and :8404/stats shows live backend state.

lessons.title: global, defaults, frontend, backend
paragraphs: An HAProxy config has sections: `global` (process-wide settings), `defaults` (inherited defaults), `frontend` (what to listen on and how to route), and `backend` (the server pool and policy). A `listen` section combines a frontend and backend in one.
This frontend/backend split is HAProxy's core model: a frontend accepts connections and selects a backend; the backend load-balances across its servers.
lessons.example: frontend accepts + routes; backend holds the servers and the balance policy.
lessons.pitfall: Putting server lines in a frontend instead of a backend is a structural error; servers belong in backend/listen sections.

question.prompt: HAProxy servers are declared in a:

lessons.title: Active health checks
paragraphs: Adding `check` to a server line turns on active health checking: HAProxy periodically probes the server and removes it from rotation when it fails. `inter` sets the interval, `fall` the failures before marking it down, `rise` the successes before marking it up again.
`option httpchk GET /health` plus `http-check expect status 200` makes the probe a real HTTP request against a health endpoint, catching an app that is listening but broken — not just a dead port.
lessons.example: server web1 web1:80 check inter 2s fall 3 rise 2  # active HTTP health checks
lessons.pitfall: Using only a TCP `check` (no httpchk) marks an app healthy as long as the port is open, even when it returns 500s.

question.prompt: `option httpchk GET /health` makes the health check:

lessons.title: Balance policies and timeouts
paragraphs: `balance` sets the algorithm: roundrobin, leastconn, source (hash by client IP for affinity), uri (hash by URL), and more. Timeouts (`timeout connect/client/server`) and `retries` bound how long and how often HAProxy waits and retries.
Sensible timeouts are mandatory: HAProxy will warn loudly about a config with no timeouts, because an unbounded server timeout can exhaust connections.
lessons.example: balance leastconn; timeout server 30s; retries 2
lessons.pitfall: Omitting `timeout server`/`timeout client` makes HAProxy warn and risks hung connections piling up.

question.prompt: `balance source` provides:

lessons.title: The stats page and running it
paragraphs: HAProxy's built-in stats page (a `listen stats` section with `stats enable` / `stats uri`) gives a live dashboard of every frontend, backend and server: state, sessions, bytes, health. It is invaluable for seeing balancing and failures in real time.
You run HAProxy in Docker by mounting the config into the official `haproxy` image and validate it with `haproxy -c -f /usr/local/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg` before starting.
lessons.example: listen stats { bind *:8404; stats enable; stats uri /stats }  # live dashboard
lessons.pitfall: Exposing the stats page on a public interface without auth leaks backend topology and metrics to anyone.

steps: Create the network and whoami backends (web1, web2) as in the NGINX lab.

Save the downloaded lb-haproxy.cfg and run `docker run -d --name hap --network lb -p 8081:80 -p 8404:8404 -v $PWD/lb-haproxy.cfg:/usr/local/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg:ro haproxy:3.0` (host port 8081 avoids clashing with the NGINX lab).
Validate with `docker exec hap haproxy -c -f /usr/local/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg`, then curl :8081 and open :8404/stats.

courses.title: 6. Kubernetes load balancing: Services and MetalLB
courses.summary: How a Kubernetes Service load-balances across pods, the ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer types, kube-proxy, and MetalLB for bare-metal external IPs.
courses.code:
# A Service load-balances across the pods matching its selector. type: LoadBalancer
# asks the platform for an external IP; on bare metal or kind that needs MetalLB.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer        # <pending> until MetalLB (or a cloud LB) assigns an address
  selector:
    app: web                # routes to every pod labelled app=web
  ports:
    - port: 80              # the Service port
      targetPort: 80        # the container port on the pods (traefik/whoami listens on 80)
---
# MetalLB gives type: LoadBalancer a real IP on bare metal / kind (metallb.io/v1beta1).
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 172.18.255.200-172.18.255.250   # MUST be inside the cluster node subnet
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: L2Advertisement
metadata:
  name: l2
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - pool
courses.expected: With MetalLB installed, `kubectl get svc web` shows an EXTERNAL-IP from the pool (not <pending>), and requests to it are spread across the app=web pods.

lessons.title: The Service abstraction
paragraphs: A Kubernetes Service is a stable virtual address in front of a set of pods chosen by a label selector. Pods are ephemeral — they come and go with changing IPs — so the Service gives clients one durable name and load-balances across the current healthy pods.
The Service's selector (e.g. app=web) must match the pods' labels. A Service with a selector that matches no pods has no endpoints and silently drops traffic.
lessons.example: A Service load-balances to all pods whose labels match its selector.
lessons.pitfall: A Service whose selector doesn't match any pod labels gets zero endpoints and quietly fails every request.

question.prompt: A Service selects its target pods by:

lessons.title: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer
paragraphs: ClusterIP (the default) gives a Service an internal-only virtual IP reachable from inside the cluster. NodePort additionally opens the same port on every node's IP. LoadBalancer asks the underlying platform for an external load balancer / IP that fronts the Service.

On a cloud provider, type LoadBalancer provisions a cloud LB automatically. On bare metal or a local kind cluster there is no cloud LB, so the Service stays <pending> until something like MetalLB provides the address.
lessons.example: ClusterIP (internal) -> NodePort (node:port) -> LoadBalancer (external IP).
lessons.pitfall: Expecting type: LoadBalancer to get an external IP on kind or bare metal without MetalLB leaves it stuck in <pending> forever.

question.prompt: On a local kind cluster, type: LoadBalancer without MetalLB stays:
question.explanation: No cloud LB to assign an IP.

lessons.title: kube-proxy and EndpointSlices
paragraphs: The control plane tracks which pods back a Service as EndpointSlices (updated as pods pass/fail readiness). kube-proxy on each node programs the data path (iptables or IPVS rules) so that traffic to the Service's ClusterIP is distributed across those endpoints.
This is L4 load balancing inside the cluster — connection-level, roughly even. It is not application-aware; path/host routing needs an L7 layer (next course).
lessons.example: EndpointSlices list healthy pods; kube-proxy programs the node to spread traffic to them.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming a Service does L7 (path/host) routing is wrong — a Service is L4; use Gateway API/Ingress for L7.

question.prompt: A Kubernetes Service load-balances at:

lessons.title: MetalLB for bare metal
paragraphs: MetalLB implements type: LoadBalancer for clusters without a cloud provider. You give it a pool of IP addresses (IPAddressPool) and an advertisement mode: L2 mode (L2Advertisement) answers ARP for the service IPs from one node, while BGP mode advertises routes to your network.
The pool must live in a routable range the cluster can own. On kind, that means an address range inside the Docker 'kind' network subnet (check `docker network inspect kind`).
lessons.example: IPAddressPool (the IPs) + L2Advertisement (announce them) = external IPs on bare metal.
lessons.pitfall: Configuring a MetalLB pool outside the node network's subnet means the assigned IPs are never reachable.

question.prompt: A MetalLB IPAddressPool must contain addresses that are:

options.text: within the cluster node network's subnet

question.explanation: They must be routable to the nodes.

steps: Create a cluster (`kind create cluster`) or use k3d/k3s (which ships a built-in ServiceLB).
Install MetalLB, then apply an IPAddressPool whose range sits inside `docker network inspect kind` subnet, plus an L2Advertisement.
Apply this Service (with a Deployment labelled app=web behind it) and run `kubectl get svc web` to see the EXTERNAL-IP.
On Docker Desktop for Mac the IP may be unreachable from the host — curl it from a container on the kind network, or use `kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80`.

courses.title: 7. Kubernetes L7 routing: the Gateway API
courses.summary: Layer-7 HTTP routing in Kubernetes with the modern Gateway API (HTTPRoute), and why Ingress is now feature-frozen after ingress-nginx's retirement.
courses.code:
# Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1, GA) is the modern L7 routing standard,
# the successor to Ingress. A Gateway defines a listener; HTTPRoute defines the rules.
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: web-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example-gateway-class   # provided by your installed Gateway controller
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: web-route
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: web-gateway                     # attach this route to the Gateway above
  hostnames:
    - "shop.example.com"
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /api                     # route /api/* to the api Service
      backendRefs:
        - name: api
          port: 80
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /                        # everything else to the web Service
      backendRefs:
        - name: web
          port: 80
courses.expected: With a Gateway controller installed, requests to shop.example.com/api/* reach the api Service and all other paths reach the web Service, routed by the single Gateway address.

lessons.title: Why L7 routing in the cluster
paragraphs: A Service (L4) can expose one app, but real clusters host many services behind one address and route by hostname and path: shop.example.com to the shop, /api to the API. That is layer-7 routing, done by an in-cluster reverse proxy driven by Kubernetes objects.

Historically this was the Ingress resource plus an Ingress controller. The routing rules live in Kubernetes objects; a controller watches them and configures the underlying proxy (Envoy, NGINX, etc.).
lessons.example: One external address -> route by Host/path to many Services (L7).
lessons.pitfall: Trying to do host/path routing with plain Services (L4) is impossible; you need an L7 layer.

lessons.title: Ingress is now feature-frozen
paragraphs: The Ingress API still exists and works, but it is feature-frozen: active development has moved to the Gateway API. Importantly, the widely-used community ingress-nginx controller was retired and its repository archived read-only in March 2026 — no further releases or security fixes.

So for new clusters, prefer the Gateway API. If you must keep Ingress, use a maintained controller (for example F5's separate NGINX Ingress Controller, Traefik, or HAProxy), not the retired community ingress-nginx.
lessons.example: Ingress = GA but frozen; community ingress-nginx retired (archived March 2026). Prefer Gateway API.
lessons.pitfall: Standing up the community ingress-nginx controller on a new cluster in 2026 adopts an unmaintained, security-frozen project.

lessons.title: Gateway, GatewayClass and HTTPRoute
paragraphs: The Gateway API splits responsibilities across roles. A GatewayClass is the installed implementation (like a StorageClass). A Gateway is an instance with listeners (ports/protocols), owned by the cluster operator. An HTTPRoute holds the routing rules and is owned by app teams, attaching to a Gateway via parentRefs.
This separation lets platform teams own the entry point while app teams own their own routes, and `backendRefs` points each rule at a Service and port.
lessons.example: GatewayClass (implementation) -> Gateway (listeners) -> HTTPRoute (rules -> backendRefs).
lessons.pitfall: Creating an HTTPRoute with no `parentRefs` to a Gateway leaves it attached to nothing and routing no traffic.

lessons.title: Routing rules and matches
paragraphs: An HTTPRoute lists rules, each with matches (path prefix/exact, headers, methods, query params) and backendRefs (one or more Services, optionally weighted for canary/traffic-splitting). The controller programs the proxy to enforce them.
Weighted backendRefs make progressive delivery first-class: send 90% of traffic to v1 and 10% to v2, then shift. This was awkward with plain Ingress and is native to the Gateway API.
lessons.example: Weighted backendRefs (90/10) enable canary releases natively in the Gateway API.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming path matches are evaluated top-to-bottom like a script is wrong — Gateway API has defined precedence (e.g. longest prefix), so order the rules to match it.

courses.title: 8. Capstone: a load-balanced, auto-scaling app
courses.summary: Combine a Deployment, a Service, health probes and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler into a resilient, self-scaling, load-balanced service.
courses.code:
# A complete, load-balanced, self-scaling service: a Deployment of replicas with
# health probes, a Service that load-balances across them, and an HPA that scales
# the replica count on CPU. (Labels/selectors/ports are cross-consistent.)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web                      # must equal the pod template labels below
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: traefik/whoami:v1.10
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80     # matches the Service targetPort
          readinessProbe:           # out of rotation until ready
            httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:            # restart if wedged
            httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m } # the HPA scales against this request
            limits:   { cpu: 250m }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: web                        # matches the pod labels
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80                # matches containerPort
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70    # add pods when average CPU exceeds 70%
courses.expected: `kubectl apply` creates a 2-replica Deployment behind a load-balancing Service; under load the HPA raises replicas toward 10 (CPU > 70%), and the Service immediately balances across the new, ready pods.

lessons.title: The Deployment and its pods
paragraphs: A Deployment manages a replica set of identical pods, recreating them if they die and rolling them out on updates. Its selector.matchLabels must equal the pod template's labels, or the API rejects it.

Those same labels are what the Service selects, so the three label sets — Deployment selector, pod template, Service selector — must agree. A mismatch gives you pods with no Service, or a Service with no pods.
lessons.example: Deployment selector.matchLabels == pod template labels == Service selector.
lessons.pitfall: A Service selector that doesn't match the Deployment's pod labels yields an endpointless Service that drops all traffic.

question.prompt: A Deployment's selector.matchLabels must equal:

lessons.title: Health probes in the loop
paragraphs: Readiness and liveness probes make load balancing safe. A pod that fails readiness is removed from the Service's endpoints (no traffic) without being killed; a pod that fails liveness is restarted. The Service only ever sends traffic to ready pods.
This is what makes zero-downtime rollouts work: a new pod joins the Service only once it passes readiness, and an old pod is drained before termination.
lessons.example: Service endpoints = only pods passing readiness; failed liveness -> restart.
lessons.pitfall: Skipping a readiness probe sends traffic to pods that are still starting up, causing errors during every rollout.

question.prompt: A pod failing its readiness probe is:
question.explanation: Taken out of rotation, not killed.

lessons.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
paragraphs: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler (autoscaling/v2) watches a metric — here average CPU utilization against the pods' CPU requests — and adjusts the Deployment's replica count between minReplicas and maxReplicas to hold the target.

It needs the metrics-server (or a custom metrics source) installed to read pod metrics, and it needs the container to declare resource requests, because utilization is measured relative to the request.
lessons.example: HPA scales replicas to keep average CPU near 70% of the request; needs metrics-server.
lessons.pitfall: An HPA on CPU utilization with no CPU request set on the container cannot compute utilization and will not scale.

question.prompt: A CPU-utilization HPA requires the container to declare:
question.explanation: Utilization is relative to the request.

lessons.title: The pieces working together
paragraphs: Under load: CPU rises, the HPA adds pods, the Deployment schedules them, each new pod passes readiness and is added to the Service's endpoints, and kube-proxy immediately balances traffic to it. When load falls, the HPA scales back down and pods are drained.
This closed loop — Deployment for lifecycle, Service for balancing, probes for health, HPA for scale — is the standard pattern for a resilient Kubernetes workload.
lessons.example: Load up -> HPA adds pods -> readiness passes -> Service balances to them -> load down -> scale in.
lessons.pitfall: Setting maxReplicas without cluster capacity (or a cluster autoscaler) leaves new pods Pending and the service still overloaded.

question.prompt: A new pod starts receiving balanced traffic once it:

options.text: passes readiness and joins the Service endpoints

steps: Apply the manifest to a cluster that has metrics-server (and MetalLB or a cloud LB for the external IP).
Confirm two ready pods, a Service with endpoints, and `kubectl get hpa web` showing the current/target CPU.
Generate load, e.g. `kubectl run -it --rm --restart=Never load --image=busybox -- /bin/sh -c 'while true; do wget -q -O- http://web; done'`, and watch replicas rise.
Stop the load and confirm the HPA scales back toward minReplicas, with the Service always balancing across ready pods.
